'''Edward Carroll Stone Jr.''' (January 23, 1936 – June 9, 2024) was an American space physicist, professor of physics at the [[California Institute of Technology]], and director of the [[NASA]] [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]] (JPL) from 1991 to 2001. He was the project scientist of the [[Voyager program]], which sent two spacecraft to the outer Solar System's giant planets and became the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space.

Stone led the Voyager mission for 50 years, from 1972 until his retirement in 2022, overseeing the spacecraft's encounters with Jupiter (1979), Saturn (1980–1981), Uranus (1986) and Neptune (1989). Under his leadership, the mission discovered active volcanism on Jupiter's moon Io, new moons and ring systems. The Voyagers continued beyond the planets to cross the heliopause and enter the interstellar medium, with Voyager 1 becoming the first spacecraft to leave the Solar System in 2012, followed by Voyager 2 in 2018. The Voyager mission became the longest-running NASA mission, with Stone being its face and advocate.

As JPL director, Stone oversaw the successful launches of [[Mars Pathfinder]] with the first Mars rover ''[[Sojourner (rover)|Sojourner]]'', [[Mars Global Surveyor]], [[Cassini–Huygens]]   and other missions during NASA's [["Faster, better, cheaper" approach|"faster, better, cheaper" era]]. Throughout his career, he served as principal investigator on nine NASA spacecraft missions, including [[SAMPEX]], the [[Advanced Composition Explorer]] and scientific instruments on the ''[[Galileo (spacecraft)|Galileo]]'' and [[STEREO]] missions.

Stone's contributions to space science earned him the [[National Medal of Science]] (1991), the [[NASA Distinguished Public Service Medal]] (2013), and the [[Shaw Prize]] in Astronomy (2019). He was elected to the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] in 1984 and played key roles in establishing major astronomical facilities, including overseeing the creation of the [[Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory]] (LIGO) during his tenure as chair of Caltech's Division of Physics, Mathematics and Astronomy, and supervising the construction of the [[W. M. Keck Observatory]].

== Early life and education ==
Edward Carroll Stone Jr. was born in [[Knoxville, Iowa]], on January 23, 1936, to Edward Carroll Stone Sr., a construction superintendent, and later a garage-door-installation company owner, and Ferne Elizabeth Stone ({{nee}} Baber), a bookkeeper.<ref name=wsj_obit/><ref name=telegraph/> He was the elder of two sons.<ref name=telegraph/> Stone grew up in [[Burlington, Iowa|Burlington]]. While at school he worked at a [[J.C. Penney]] department store and was a member of the Burlington Municipal Band playing [[French horn]].<ref name="jpl obit" />

Stone studied at [[Burlington Junior College]] in Iowa, and continued his education at the [[University of Chicago]], where he earned his [[Master of Science|M.S.]] (1959) and [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] (1964) degrees in physics.<ref name=telegraph/> Initially, he planned to study [[nuclear physics]], but became interested in [[space physics]] after the launch of the Soviet [[Sputnik]] in 1957.<ref name=nature2/> Stone began astrophysics research in 1961, working on a cosmic-ray telescope carried by the [[Discoverer 36]] spy satellite. He worked on it under the cosmic-ray researcher [[John Alexander Simpson|John A. Simpson]]'s supervision.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-024-02285-w|title=Edward C. Stone obituary: physicist who guided Voyager probes to interstellar space|first=Alan C.|last=Cummings|date=July 10, 2024|journal=Nature|volume=631|issue=8021|page=501|via=www.nature.com|doi=10.1038/d41586-024-02285-w|bibcode=2024Natur.631..501C |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name="jpl obit" /> The experiment became his PhD thesis, titled ''Low energy cosmic-ray protons''.<ref>{{cite thesis |title=Low energy cosmic-ray protons |first=Edward |last=Stone |institution=[[University of Chicago]] |year=1964 |oclc=49431918}}</ref> While in Chicago, Stone also worked with [[Eugene Parker]]; he said later that "Parker taught me how to reduce a problem to its nuts and bolts, to a picture."<ref name=profile>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1990/05/20/magazine/his-head-in-the-stars.html|title=His Head In The Stars|first=Michael |last=Norman|work=The New York Times |date=May 20, 1990|via=NYTimes.com |archive-url=https://archive.today/20250519064159/https://www.nytimes.com/1990/05/20/magazine/his-head-in-the-stars.html |archive-date=19 May 2025}}</ref>

== Caltech ==
Stone moved to Caltech to work on space physics with [[Rochus Eugen Vogt]] in 1964,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.shawprize.org/autobiography/edward-c-stone/|title=Edward C Stone|website=The Shaw Prize}}</ref> and helped him establish the [[Space Radiation Laboratory (Caltech)|Space Radiation Laboratory]].<ref name=airspace/> He became a full faculty member in 1967.<ref name="nyt obit" /> In 1976, Stone was named professor of physics, later the David Morrisroe Professor of Physics,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://beacon.jpl.nasa.gov/exhibits/directors/Stone.html |title=Edward Stone Profile |work=NASA |access-date=May 12, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100527202155/http://beacon.jpl.nasa.gov/exhibits/directors/Stone.html |archive-date=May 27, 2010 }}</ref> and was chair of the Division of Physics, Mathematics, and Astronomy from 1983 to 1988;<ref name="nyt obit" /> during his tenure he oversaw the establishment of the [[Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory]] (LIGO).<ref name=caltech/> He also served as director of the Caltech Space Radiation Laboratory, and as vice president for Astronomical Facilities. He was the vice-chair of the [[Thirty meter telescope|Thirty Meter Telescope]] Board of Directors.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.tmt.org/about-tmt/board-directors |title=TMT Board of Directors |access-date=May 30, 2017 |archive-date=December 18, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131218113212/http://www.tmt.org/about-tmt/board-directors }}</ref> He also served on the board of the [[California Association for Research in Astronomy]] (CARA) for nearly 25 years, and oversaw the construction of the [[W. M. Keck Observatory]].<ref name=caltech/> He was also a [[W. M. Keck Foundation]] director, and chaired the Keck Foundation's Science and Engineering Committee for 24 years.<ref name=keck/>

== Voyager program ==
In 1964, [[Gary Flandro]], a summer student at JPL, found out that a rare planetary alignment of the giant planets would allow a mission he called "[[Grand Tour program|the Grand Tour]]". Such an alignment occurs every 175 years; Flandro calculated that the best option was to launch spacecraft in 1977. [[Gravity assist]] maneuvers were already known, but according to Flandro he was the first to notice the opportunity to visit the giant planets.{{efn|According to Flandro, many experts were sceptical and didn't believe that such mission was possible: "After we had discovered this mission design, I consulted experts at JPL to find out whether they thought we had a workable notion. They showed no interest in the outer planets and proceeded to explain the many impossibilities confronting such missions. The guidance guys said, "No, you can't guide accurately enough." The spacecraft design people said, "No, you can't build a spacecraft that would survive long enough to do this." The data people proclaimed that "You can't transmit any useful data over interplanetary distances (and think of the time delay between transmission and receipt of the signal)." Every expert I consulted had a negative response. You know, they said, "You can't get through the asteroid belt. A spacecraft cannot survive passing through the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter without colliding with something." Another problem voiced was that "spacecraft electronics cannot survive passage through Jupiter's magnetic field," On-and-on the negative responses built up. They declared, "You just cannot do that. Come on, kid don't bother us anymore." That inspired me to work a little bit harder on selling this whole thing."<ref name=flandro/>}} NASA was reluctant to finance the proposed mission of four spacecraft, but the proposal eventually transformed into the [[Voyager program]].<ref name=flandro>{{cite web |url=https://heritageproject.caltech.edu/interviews-updates/gary-flandro |title=Gary Flandro (PHD '67), Aerospace Engineer |date=September 7, 2022 }}</ref>

[[File:Voyager first science meeting, 1972.jpg|thumb|Stone (front row, second from left) at the Voyager first science meeting, 1972]]

In 1972, Stone became the project scientist for the Voyager program that sent two space probes to the giant planets in the outer [[Solar System]].<ref name="jpl obit" /> He was invited for the position by [[Harris "Bud" Schurmeier]], the mission's first project manager;<ref name=flandro/><ref name=planetary>{{Cite web|url=https://www.planetary.org/articles/stories_stone|title=The Stories Behind the Voyager Mission: Ed Stone|website=The Planetary Society}}</ref> according to Schurmeier, Stone was proposed as the project scientist by Rochus Vogt, who was involved in the Grand Tour mission planning from the start. Stone himself was reluctant at first: as a scientist, he didn't want to sacrifice a lot of time for administrative work.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.planetary.org/articles/stories_schurmeier|title=The Stories Behind the Voyager Mission: Bud Schurmeier|website=The Planetary Society}}</ref>{{efn|According to [[Louis Friedman]], a friend of both Stone and Schurmeier, who was involved in the Grand Tour program planning before it was transformed into Voyager: "Bud Schurmeier was a phenomenal person. He is the one who made the mission happen – he and his teams: spacecraft and mission. Ed without Bud wouldn't have done anything, and Bud without Ed wouldn't have [laugh] achieved the great results. But either of them without the support of the rest of the teams would also have not been able to do it alone. Voyager has many heroes. None, more than Bud Schurmeier."<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://heritageproject.caltech.edu/interviews/louis-friedman|title=Louis Friedman|website=Heritage Project}}</ref>}} Stone was also the [[principal investigator]] for the [[Cosmic Ray Subsystem]] experiment on both Voyager spacecraft.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/experiment/display.action?id=1977-084A-08|title=NASA – NSSDCA – Experiment – Details|website=nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov|access-date=May 30, 2017}}</ref>

Stone supervised the work of 11 teams of about 200 scientists;<ref name=streeter>{{cite news |url= http://www.latimes.com/news/local/la-me-0414-ed-stone-20110412,0,4527527.story |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110417233039/http://www.latimes.com/news/local/la-me-0414-ed-stone-20110412,0,4527527.story |archive-date= April 17, 2011 |title= A new frontier in quest to understand the cosmos |last= Streeter |first= Kurt |date= April 14, 2011 |work= Los Angeles Times |access-date= April 14, 2011}}</ref> he organized "the clique-like teams" and work groups for key points of interest, "moons, rings, atmosphere and magnetosphere". Stone had the final word on observation target selection, instrument usage, and the spacecraft trajectories.<ref name=nature2>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/497424a |title=Voyager: Outward bound |date=2013 |last1=Witze |first1=Alexandra |journal=Nature |volume=497 |issue=7450 |pages=424–427 |pmid=23698425 |bibcode=2013Natur.497..424W }}</ref><ref name=turf/> A NASA official who was present at the first Voyager meeting, observed that "Stone knew more about every one of their instruments than the P.I.s themselves knew."<ref name=turf/>

[[File:P-24049Dc Ed Stone.jpg|thumb|Stone during a press conference in the 1980s]]

Stone also became a spokesman for Voyager, and became well known to the public in the 1980s, after he held dozens of press conferences announcing Voyagers' discoveries.{{efn|See more on press conferences in {{harvnb|Butrica|2001}}, search for "The press conference was a keystone activity of the Project Scientist..."}}<ref name=jpl>{{cite web |title=Dr. Edward C. Stone (1935–2004) |url=https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/who-we-are/faces-of-leadership-the-directors-of-jpl/dr-edward-c-stone-1936/ |website=Jet Propulsion Laboratory}}</ref> According to the Voyager project manager [[Norman Haynes]], Stone "revolutionized the world of project science".<ref name=profile/><ref name="nyt obit"/>

Stone said that planetary encounters and the discovery of [[volcanism on Io]] were the most memorable events of the Voyager mission for him. He recounted the team's regular work process:<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-017-0339-2|title=The Voyagers|first=Ed|last=Stone|date=December 22, 2017|journal=Nature Astronomy|volume=1|issue=12|page=896|via=www.nature.com|doi=10.1038/s41550-017-0339-2|bibcode=2017NatAs...1..896S |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://science.nasa.gov/people/ed-stone/|title=Ed Stone - NASA Science}}</ref>

{{Blockquote|text=There was a regular routine: In the afternoon we had a science meeting where individuals would say, "This is what we've seen" or "This is what we think" or "This is what we don't understand." Members from all 11 science teams participated, packing the conference room. These daily science meetings were a form of real time peer review that was also a way to choose which observations to report at the press conference the following morning. After the meeting, I would work with the investigators in outlining graphical illustrations that could be prepared overnight for use at the press conference at 10 a.m. In parallel, the imaging team would choose the images and prepare the captions for those that would be printed overnight for distribution to the reporters gathered at JPL. That afternoon, we would do it all over again with another day of observations and analyses.}}

[[Stephen P. Synnott]] recounted how Stone let him name a moon of Jupiter that he discovered on Voyager photos in 1980, saying "it looks like you've found yourself a moon" after checking the calculations. Synnott chose [[Thebe (moon)|Thebe]] from a list of names suggested by the [[IAU]].<ref>{{Cite magazine |url=https://time.com/6987877/ed-stone-death-remembrance/ |title=Godspeed, Ed Stone—the Man Who Showed Us the Solar System|first=Jeffrey|last=Kluger|date=June 12, 2024|magazine=TIME}}</ref>

{{Quote box
 | quote  = Becoming Voyager project scientist was the best decision I made in my life.<ref name="jpl obit"/>

[the Project Scientist served] an impedance matching function between the engineering requirements and constraints and the science requirements and constraints to try to find a way to achieve the optimum match between these two different sets of requirements and desirements.<ref name=butrica>{{cite book |url=https://www.nasa.gov/history/SP-4219/Chapter11.html |editor=Pamela E. Mack |first=Andrew J. |last=Butrica |title=From Engineering Science to Big Science: The NACA and NASA Collier Trophy Research Project Winners |chapter=Voyager: The Grand Tour of Big Science |year=2001 |publisher=NASA}}</ref>
 | width  = 30%
 | align  = right
}}

Stone was the main advocate and salesman of the Voyagers.<ref name=wsj_obit>{{Cite web|url=https://www.wsj.com/science/space-astronomy/ed-stone-scientist-voyager-mission-dies-at-88-44c65bc4|title=Ed Stone, Top Scientist—and Salesman—for the Voyager Mission, Dies at 88|first=Chris|last=Kornelis|date=July 10, 2024|website=The Wall Street Journal}}</ref> After the last planetary encounter he was able to receive funding for an extended mission, the Voyager Interstellar Mission. The Voyagers became the only spacecraft that left Solar System into [[interstellar space]].<ref name=franklin>{{Cite web|url=https://fi.edu/en/awards/laureates/edward-c-stone|title=Edward C. Stone &#124; The Franklin Institute|date=November 23, 2021|website=fi.edu}}</ref><ref name=turf>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/12/20/magazine/edward-stone-nasa.html|title=How Edward Stone Resolved NASA's Scientific Turf Wars|first=Jon|last=Gertner|work=The New York Times |date=December 20, 2024}}</ref>

Jamie Sue Rankin became Stone's last PhD student. Her thesis was on the Voyagers' interstellar space data; she graduated in 2018 and became the Voyagers' deputy project scientist in 2022. Before Rankin, Stone refused to advise graduate students for about 25 years.<ref name=rankin>{{Cite web|url=https://www.princeton.edu/news/2022/12/15/nasas-voyager-next-generation|title=NASA's Voyager: The next generation|website=princeton.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://science.nasa.gov/people/jamie-rankin/|title=Jamie Rankin - NASA Science}}</ref> Later, Rankin became the Voyager's deputy project scientist.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.princeton.edu/news/2022/12/15/nasas-voyager-next-generation|title=NASA’s Voyager: The next generation|website=www.princeton.edu}}</ref>

The Voyager mission visited all four giant planets and is the only spacecraft that visited Uranus and Neptune. It is NASA's longest-running spacecraft mission. In 2022, Stone retired after holding the role of the Voyager project scientist for 50 years.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Edward Stone Retires After 50 Years as NASA Voyager's Project Scientist |url=https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/edward-stone-retires-after-50-years-as-nasa-voyagers-project-scientist |access-date=2022-11-13 |website=NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) |archive-date=November 11, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221111085809/https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/edward-stone-retires-after-50-years-as-nasa-voyagers-project-scientist |url-status=live }}</ref>

Simultaneously with being the Voyager's project scientist, Stone taught first-year physics at Caltech, using examples from it: "The wonderful thing about planetary fly-bys is there’s a lot of freshman physics that you can talk about: the encounters, the trajectories."<ref name=wsj_obit/>

== JPL ==
[[File:P39582 2 Ed Stone.jpg|thumb|Stone with a Voyager model in 1992]]

Though Stone is better known as the Voyager's project scientist, he served as a [[principal investigator]] for multiple other missions.{{efn|Multiple sources, including NASA, often say that Stone was the PI of nine NASA spacecraft missions and co-investigator on five more,<ref name="jpl obit">{{cite web |title=Ed Stone, Former Director of JPL and Voyager Project Scientist, Dies |url=https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/ed-stone-former-director-of-jpl-and-voyager-project-scientist-dies/ |website=JPL Life |publisher=Jet Propulsion Laboratory |date=June 11, 2024}}</ref> but don't list these missions. Stone himself said that "[Before Voyager] My first space mission was in 1961 and I had flown instruments on missions in 1965, '67, '69, '72, and '73 – so I had lots of instruments in space, but they had all been on Earth-orbiters."<ref name=planetary/>}} He was the PI of the Cosmic Ray Experiment on [[Orbiting Geophysical Observatory]]-6 (OGO-6, 1969), the PI of the Electrons and Hydrogen and Helium Isotopes experiments on [[Explorer 47|Interplanetary Monitoring Platform 7]] (IMP-7, 1972)<ref name=airspace>{{Cite web|url=https://airandspace.si.edu/stories/editorial/dr-edward-c-stones-contributions-aerospace|title=Dr. Edward C. Stone's Contributions to Aerospace|date=July 19, 2024|website=airandspace.si.edu}}</ref> and [[IMP-8]] (1973),<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nasa.gov/nssdc/|title=NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive Status - NASA}}</ref> was involved into the cancelled [[Particle Astrophysics Magnet Facility|ASTROMAG]] (1980s),<ref name=profile/> was the PI of two instruments of the cancelled [[International Solar Polar Mission]] (1981),<ref name=sampex/> the PI of a heavy-ion counter on the ''[[Galileo (spacecraft)|Galileo]]'' mission to Jupiter (1989),<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/galileo-scientific-result-release/|title=Galileo Scientific Result Release|website=NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) |year=1989}}</ref> the PI of [[SAMPEX]] (1992),<ref name=sampex>{{Cite journal|title=A Small Pathbreaking Spacecraft: Giants of Space Research (Bernard Blake, Dieter Hovestadt, and Edward Stone)|first1=D. N.|last1=Baker|first2=G. M.|last2=Mason|date=May 23, 2025|journal=Perspectives of Earth and Space Scientists|volume=6|issue=1|article-number=e2024CN000270|doi=10.1029/2024CN000270|doi-access=free}}</ref> the PI for the [[Advanced Composition Explorer]] (1997),<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://izw1.caltech.edu/ACE/ace_personnel.html|title=ACE Personnel|website=izw1.caltech.edu}}</ref><ref name=profile/> and co-investigator of [[STEREO]] mission's High Energy Telescope (HET) and Low Energy Telescope (LET) (both part of the In-situ Measurements of Particles and CME Transients (IMPACT) instrument package) (2006).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sprg.ssl.berkeley.edu/impact/impact_team.html|title=STEREO/IMPACT – IMPACT Team |website=sprg.ssl.berkeley.edu}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |url= https://authors.library.caltech.edu/records/xz7ge-1h388|title=The High Energy Telescopes for the STEREO Mission |bibcode=2008ICRC....1..103V |last1=von Rosenvinge |first1=T. T. |last2=Cummings |first2=A. C. |last3=Leske |first3=R. A. |last4=Mewaldt |first4=R. A. |last5=Reames |first5=D. V. |last6=Stone |first6=E. C. |last7=Wiedenbeck |first7=M. E. |journal=International Cosmic Ray Conference |date=2008 |volume=1 |page=103 }}</ref> Stone also "oversaw the redesign of the cooling system" on the [[Spitzer Space Telescope]] (2003),<ref name=caltech/> and was an investigator on the [[Integrated Science Investigation of the Sun]] instrument on the [[Parker Solar Probe]] (2018).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.eoportal.org/satellite-missions/psp|title=PSP (Parker Solar Probe) |publisher=eoPortal}}</ref>

In 1991, Ed Stone–a well-known, enthusiastic and respectable scientist–was made the JPL director.<ref name=stone_years>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YXSxmgVLhskC |chapter=Part III. Beyond the Cold War: The Stone Years, 1991–2001 |title=Into the Black: JPL and the American Space Program, 1976–2004 |isbn=978-0-300-13458-2 |last1=Westwick |first1=Peter J. |date=October 2008 |publisher=Yale University Press }}</ref>{{rp|207}} His directorship was during the difficult period of the 90s: with the [[Cold War]] and the [[Space Race]] between the US and the USSR finished, NASA saw dwindling budgets and introduced the so-called [["Faster, better, cheaper" approach|"faster, better, cheaper" approach]], that encouraged smaller, cheaper missions built with the help of third-party contractors, efficiently "commercializing" the research lab and forcing it to work with industry.<ref name=stone_years/>{{rp|208, 254}} Cost-cutting had to be done by Stone, who tried to adapt a new management culture at JPL, while at the same time trying not to hurt science.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1997-05-11-op-57676-story.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20250602213154/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1997-05-11-op-57676-story.html |archive-date=2 June 2025 |title=Edward Stone |website=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=11 May 1997 }}</ref> The plans were to downsize the lab and fire around 30% of JPL personnel by the end of the decade; Stone and Caltech leadership even feared that JPL could be closed.<ref name=stone_years/>{{rp|208–209}}

The "faster, better, cheaper" (FBC) approach was described as:<ref name=fbc>{{cite journal |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0094576500000990 |doi=10.1016/S0094-5765(00)00099-0 |bibcode=2000AcAau..47..607D |title=Faster, Better, Cheaper: An Institutional View |last1=Dumas |first1=Larry N. |last2=Walton |first2=Amy L. |journal=Acta Astronautica |date=2000 |volume=47 |issue=2 |page=607 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

{{blockquote|Faster applies to project development time, which for convenience can be defined as the period from project approval to launch. Rapid development cycles help control costs and enable the incorporation of the latest advances in technology, because the design freeze date is closer to the launch date. Better applies to the capability of the flight system as a scientific instrument, improvement here is based on the use of advanced technologies, and on better-focused science based on the knowledge gained from earlier exploration missions. Finally, cheaper denotes both lower cost per mission and, through clever design and use of technology, more effective use of available funds.}}

JPL had little experience in small missions at the time: its "flagship" missions, like ''Voyager'', ''[[Cassini (spacecraft)|Cassini]]'', and ''[[Galileo (spacecraft)|Galileo]]'', employed hundreds of people for decades. Cassini, for example, "directly supported maybe 500 work-years, about 10 percent of total lab staff [and] provided close to 20 percent of the lab budget".<ref name=stone_years/>{{rp|223}} In order to comply with budget restrictions and save the mission, ''Cassini'' was downsized; to save $250 million, the scan platform had to be removed from the plans.<ref name=stone_years/>{{rp|260–261}} Stone himself saw the "faster-better-cheaper" as a cultural change of the lab's engineering practices.<ref name=stone_years/>{{rp|223}}

Stone also became a proponent of a management culture change at JPL, and installed [[Richard Laeser]] (former Voyager project manager) to apply [[total quality management]] (TQM) at all levels. Reorganization was required to meet NASA needs, and TQM "emphasized customer service", even though few people at JPL saw NASA as their customer.<ref name=stone_years/>{{rp|230–232}} Many employees were against the new management practices.<ref name=stone_years/>{{rp|223, 240}}{{efn|Before TQM and the management changes, project managers at JPL were autonomous and even autocrative: "Project managers were often hard-driving autocrats; as Voyager manager Norm Haynes put it, they "were culled out to be sort of rugged individualists." The otherwise good-natured John Casani, the epitome of the breed, was also known as the "Ayatollah Casani". At one point a consultant gave a personality test to senior managers; at one end of the scale were the counselor types, such as the professorial Stone, and at the other were what Casani called the "leg breakers", including himself."<ref name=stone_years/>{{rp|233}}}}

The most successful, "model" example of an FBC mission was the [[Mars Pathfinder]] lander and the first Mars rover, the ''[[Sojourner (rover)|Sojourner]]''. The mission cost around 200 million dollars and was widely reported in the press, appearing on the covers of ''Time'' and ''Newsweek''.<ref name=stone_years/>{{rp|267–270}} Other missions were less fortunate: in 1998–1999, six missions were launched; four of them failed, including two Mars orbiters.<ref name=stone_years/>{{rp|276}} Both JPL (Stone) and the NASA administration ([[Daniel Goldin]]) acknowledged that they pushed too far with the FBC; no project manager of the failed missions was fired.<ref name=nature2/><ref name=stone_years/>{{rp|283}}

According to Peter J. Westwick, as the director of JPL, Stone was a "cautious revolutionary". He retired in 2001; his successor, [[Charles Elachi]], "felt no need to change JPL's culture".<ref name=stone_years/>{{rp|287}}

== Retirement and death ==
Stone retired from Voyager in 2022, after holding the role for 50 years, but remained professor emeritus at Caltech. He died in Pasadena, California, on June 9, 2024, at the age of 88.<ref name="nyt obit">{{cite web|title=Edward Stone, 88, Physicist Who Oversaw Voyager Missions, Is Dead|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/06/14/science/space/edward-stone-physicist-dead.html|last=Roberts|first=Sam|date=June 14, 2024|work=The New York Times|access-date=June 14, 2024}}</ref><ref name=caltech>{{cite web |title=Edward C. Stone, 1936–2024 |date=June 11, 2024 |url=https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/edward-stone-1936-2024 |publisher=Caltech }}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Stone was a shy man, and worked 100-hour weeks at times. [[Alan C. Cummings]], the [[Cosmic Ray Subsystem]] co-investigator, who worked with Stone for fifty years, described him as "very calm ... the smartest guy I ever met. He was a multiplexer supreme."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://heritageproject.caltech.edu/interviews-updates/alan-cummings|title=Alan Cummings, Astrophysicist, Cosmic Ray Researcher, and Voyager Mission Scientist|date=July 3, 2023|website=Heritage Project}}</ref> Stone was profiled in 1990 for ''[[The New York Times]]'' by Michael Norman:<ref name=profile/>

{{Blockquote|text=A space scientist has to be a visionary, a poet in a white lab coat who can give voice to our collective craving for adventure, our fascination with a universe we have not been able to touch.

At first sight, Ed Stone is not such a man. As he hurries through the luminous California morning, one hardly notices him, 5 feet 10 inches, 130 pounds, a wisp in gray—gray suit, gray shirt, gray felt shoes{{efn|Kurt Streeter observed the same devotion to gray color in 2011, writing "He is wearing his standard work attire: gray sport jacket, gray pants, gray shoes, gray socks—and a white shirt."<ref name=streeter/>}} – lugging an ancient leather briefcase. He keeps to the shadows and side paths, terra incognita, a physicist so swept up in his daily occasions, so occupied by science, his life appears to turn on little else.

And yet, for the public, Ed Stone has been a kind of [[Cicero]] on space. As chief scientist on Project Voyager, he has participated in some 60 public briefings and news conferences over the 13 years of the project.}}

[[File:Edward Stone at JPL in 2019.jpg|thumb|Stone in 2019]]

Stone met Alice Wickliffe on a [[blind date]] at a comedy club and married her in 1962. She died in December 2023. They had two daughters, Susan and Janet. Stone was described as a "shy man, sometimes diffident, often detached"; his younger daughter compared him to ''[[Star Trek]]''{{'}}s [[Spock|Mr. Spock]]. He had no close friends but "shared a long professional kinship with several scientists". He was a registered Democrat but not very interested in politics. Norman wrote that "He has no interest in sports, no hobbies ... His main recreation is to read a daily newspaper. His favorite food is raisin pie. He is not a man of faith."<ref name=profile/>

The Voyager mission became the longest NASA mission; Stone described it in 2012:<ref name=telegraph>{{Cite web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/obituaries/2024/06/23/ed-stone-voyager-nasa-planets-obituary/|title=Ed Stone, scientist who led the Voyager space missions through the solar system and beyond – obituary |work=The Telegraph |date=June 23, 2024|via=telegraph.co.uk}}</ref>

{{Blockquote|text=When I started on Voyager my two daughters were young. By the time they were in college we had passed Saturn and were on our way to Uranus. They got married and the Voyagers just kept going, and we had grandchildren and Voyager just kept going and our grandchildren are now aware of what's happening to the Voyagers just like our children were.}}

Stone was known as "an incredibly fast walker":<ref name=wsj_obit/>
{{Quote|text=The joke was that nobody knew what he really looked like, because when he was coming toward you, he was [[blueshift]]ed and when he was going away from you, he was [[redshift]]ed.
|source=Alan Cummings}}

Stone appeared in ''[[The Farthest]]'', a 2017 documentary on the Voyager program.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt6223974/|title=The Farthest|date=August 11, 2017|via=IMDb}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
{{Multiple images
| total_width = 270
| perrow      = 1
| image1      = All Plaques Graphic-04.png
| image2      = All Plaques Graphic-05.png
| footer      = Memorial plaques on the Edward Stone Voyager Exploration Trail at JPL. See more photos on [[:commons:Category:Edward Stone Voyager Exploration Trail|Commons]].
}}

In 2002, JPL established the Edward Stone Award for Outstanding Research Publication, which is awarded annually to JPL employees in both science and engineering.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/site/research/research-community/awards-and-recognitions/ed-stone-award/|title=Office of Research and Development (ORD) &#124; The Edward Stone Award for Outstanding Research Publication|website=jpl.nasa.gov}}</ref>

In 2012, a middle school was named in Stone's honor in Burlington, his hometown.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mississippivalleypublishing.com/the_hawk_eye/ed-stone-bhs-graduate-and-top-voyager-scientist-dies-at-88/article_998c17f2-2997-11ef-8f66-dfec330bb869.html|title=Ed Stone, BHS graduate and top Voyager scientist, dies at 88|first=Julie |last=Nickell|date=June 13, 2024|website=Daily Gate City}}</ref>

In 2013, Stone was awarded the [[NASA Distinguished Public Service Medal]], the highest NASA award for non-governmental employees. NASA arranged the award ceremony to be performed during ''[[The Colbert Report]]'' night show, with the award presented by [[Stephen Colbert]] dressed in a [[retrofuturism|retrofuturistic]] spacesuit. Stone was unaware of the award when he came to the show. It was given "for a lifetime of extraordinary scientific achievement and outstanding leadership of space science missions, and for his exemplary sharing of the exciting results with the public."<ref name=colbert/>

In 2019, Stone won the [[Shaw Prize]] in Astronomy, "for his leadership in the Voyager project".<ref name=shaw/> The award included $1.2 million; Stone endowed a summer student program with this money "in return for the wonderful mission [Flandro] discovered".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2020/jan/11/voyager-scientist-ed-stone-on-the-search-for-extraterrestrial-life-we-need-to-get-back-to-enceladus|title=Voyager scientist Ed Stone on the search for extraterrestrial life: 'We need to get back to Enceladus'|first1=Hannah|last1=Devlin|work=The Guardian |date=January 11, 2020}}</ref>

In 2023, the [[W. M. Keck Foundation]] endowed the Edward C. Stone Professorship at Caltech. Christopher Martin, director of Caltech Optical Observatories, became the first Stone Professor.<ref name=keck>{{Cite web|url=https://giving.caltech.edu/news/keck-foundation-honors-edward-stone-with-endowed-professorship-at-caltech-1|title=Keck Foundation Honors Edward Stone with Endowed Professorship at Caltech|date=July 10, 2023|website=Advancement and Alumni Relations}}</ref>

In 2024, the Edward Stone Voyager Exploration Trail was unveiled at the JPL campus to commemorate Stone and his "penchant for walking". The trail starts at JPL Mall and consists of two paths, made similar to Voyager 1 and 2 trajectories. The trail features 24 memorial plaques, designed to "evoke the [[Voyager Golden Record|Golden Record]]" commemorating the mission's and Ed Stone's personal milestones.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://astrobiology.com/2024/12/nasa-jpl-unveils-the-dr-edward-stone-exploration-trail.html|title=NASA JPL Unveils The Dr. Edward Stone Exploration Trail|first=Keith|last=Cowing|date=December 9, 2024|website=Astrobiology}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/ed-stone-trail/|title=Edward Stone Voyager Exploration Trail|website=NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL)}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

[[File:Bush-voyager-16.jpg|thumb|Ed Stone and Voyager mission team members gave a framed copy of an iconic Voyager 1 solar system image that includes Earth as a "[[Pale Blue Dot]]" to President [[George H. W. Bush]] on June 7, 1990.]]
